background.definition: Pruritus ani (PA) presents with perianal itching, a common and often embarrassing problem for patients. It is most often symptomatic of an underlying condition (secondary PA). Idiopathic PA is therefore a diagnosis of exclusion.

list.listitem: Incidence data are unknown.
The best prevalence data available report PA occurring in 6 of 102 randomly selected patients.

However, studies are subject to selection bias; the dermatology research suggests that PA is most often caused by dermatologic pathology, whereas the surgical literature reports anorectal pathology as the most common cause.
See for causes of secondary PA.
The most common causes are dermatologic (thought to account for at least half) and anorectal pathologies.
Local perianal irritation and inflammation lead to scratching, which precipitates more inflammation, leading to further perianal itching.
Irritation may cause the patient to clean and scrub the area excessively, resulting in symptom exacerbation.
Self-treatment with topical medication may also cause a superimposed contact dermatitis and prolong PA.
PA presents with perianal itching, a common and often embarrassing problem for patients. C

Potential causes include the use of inciting medications or topical products, existing or prior skin and systemic disorders, food allergies, potentially allergenic items such as scented toilet paper, cleansing products, and over-the-counter regimens. B
Physical examination should include a careful inspection of the anogenital skin, including palpation of the area and a digital rectal examination. C
Consider performing colonoscopy in patients with prolonged PA, especially those older than 50 years, to rule out malignancy. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Usually a history of skin disorders manifesting in other body parts
Typically has acute onset and rapid relief with appropriate treatment; may involve genitalia
Suspected when PA is persistent without any previous clinical manifestations

list.listitem: Important items from the history include the use of potentially inciting medications or topical products. Ask also about existing or prior skin and systemic disorders and food allergies.
Inquire about other potentially allergenic items such as scented toilet paper, cleansing products, and over-the-counter regimens.
To determine whether food items may be causing PA, the patient should maintain a food diary and monitor intake of spices, citrus, coffee, tea, dairy products, chocolate, and tomatoes.
Physical examination should include a careful inspection of the anogenital skin, including palpation of the area and a digital rectal examination.
Perform an anoscopic examination when indicated to rule out abscess, hemorrhoids, and obscure lesions.
Idiopathic PA is a diagnosis of exclusion.
Consider performing or referring patients for a sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy to rule out malignancy (especially those older than 50 years with otherwise unremitting symptoms).
For suspected systemic disorders, consider obtaining fasting glucose; CBCs; liver, kidney, and thyroid function; IgE; and stool for ova and parasites.

Important items from the history include the use of potentially inciting medications or topical products. Physical examination should include a careful inspection of the anogenital skin, including palpation of the area, a digital rectal examination, and anoscopy.

Consider sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy to rule out malignancy in patients older than 50 years. Other laboratory studies to consider include glucose; CBC; liver, kidney, and thyroid function; IgE; and stool for ova and parasites.
Dermatology referral and patch testing may be necessary for persistent cases.
Oral antihistamines may provide temporary relief to limit scratching and help interrupt the itch-scratch cycle. C
Secondary PA requires treatment of the underlying condition and interruption of the itch-scratch cycle. B
Avoid skin irritation from excessive drying/wiping and/or the use of topical agents. B
Treat with 1% hydrocortisone ointment twice daily for 2 weeks, but avoid excessive use because this can cause skin sensitization and atrophy. A
Capsaicin 0.006% cream and intradermal methylene blue injection are options for refractory disease. B
Oral antihistamines may provide temporary relief to limit scratching.

Hydrocortisone 1% ointment twice daily for 2 weeks resulted in a 68% reduction from baseline itch rating on a continuous scale compared with placebo. It is important to avoid excessive use leading to skin sensitization and atrophy.
Capsaicin 0.006% cream relieved PA within 3 days in 31 of 44 patients; during follow-up, capsaicin decreased or eliminated itching when applied every 0.5 to 7 days.

In a single study, 1 month after intradermal methylene blue injection, 24 of 30 patients reported no symptoms, and, after 12 months, 23 remained symptom free. Local cellulitis accounted for the only adverse outcomes in this study. Skin necrosis and abscess were reported in prior studies.

A meta-analysis of case series found an overall good response to a single injection of methylene blue (76%) and 85% after a second injection. However, there have been no randomized trials or comparative studies.

PERINAL, a no-touch aqueous spray containing hydrocortisone and lignocaine, applied 2 to 3 times daily effectively resolved PA in 46 of 58 patients; this product is currently unavailable in the United States.
Surgical treatment for underlying conditions that lead to secondary PA, such as hemorrhoidectomy and cancer resection, may or may not result in complete resolution of PA.

Maintaining good skin hygiene, including perianal cleansing with a mild agent (eg, Protex liquid cleanse; Colgate-Palmolive) twice daily, can be as effective as corticosteroids in resolving PA within 2 weeks.
Keeping the skin dry is helpful, but avoid excessive drying and wiping.
Wear clean, absorbent, loose clothing.
Avoid topical agents (eg, powders, creams).
Regular bowel movements (high-fiber diet) may eliminate fissures, diarrhea, and leakage, which are common causes of PA.
Consider dermatology referral and patch testing to rule out contact dermatitis and other dermatologic causes.
Maintaining good skin hygiene can effectively resolve PA in most patients. B
Although specific treatment interventions may resolve PA symptoms, recurrence is common and may require intermittent retreatment. C
Strongly consider colonoscopy in patients over 50 years of age to rule out malignancy.

The primary cause of PA in children is pinworms (Enterobius vermicularis), best treated with either a single oral dose of albendazole suspension (400 mg) plus anal application with a cotton-tipped applicator or a single dose of mebendazole 100 mg orally.

list.listitem: Skin irritation (scratching and excessive cleaning)

Contact dermatitis (coffee, alcohol, peanuts, chocolate, milk, cola, citrus; medication; residual feces; applied substances, including medications used to treat PA; and sanitation items such as toilet paper and sprays)
Atopic dermatitis
Seborrheic dermatitis
Psoriasis
Lichen sclerosis
Lichen planus
Bowen’s disease
Extramammary Paget's disease
Hemorrhoids
Anal fissure
Anal fistula
Incontinence
Chronic diarrhea
Cancer (patients typically older and PA prolonged)
Proctitis
Abscess
Yeast (rule out diabetes, HIV)
Dermatophytes
Sexually transmitted disease (Condyloma acuminatum, gonorrhea, Herpes simplex, syphilis, Molluscum contagiosum)
Bacteria [Streptococcus, Staph. aureus, erythrasma (Corynebacterium minutissimum)]
Parasites [Enterobius vermicularis most common cause of PA in children, Sarcoptes scabiei (scabies), Phthirus pubis (pubic lice)]
Diabetes
Thyroid disorders
Stress
Anxiety
Depression
